At the heart of this word is one simple concept: emptiness that causes weakness or lifelessness. Not just being empty, but being so drained of what you need — nourishment, energy, substance — that you become feeble, hollow, or completely devoid of vitality.

Think of a container that has been completely drained of its contents. It doesn't just sit there neutrally empty — that emptiness has a consequence. It's useless. It has no power. That consequential emptiness is what inanition is all about.

The word carries two distinct but closely related meanings. Both are built on the same idea of draining emptiness — one is physical, one is figurative.

Meaning 1 — Physical (The Primary and More Common Meaning)

Inanition refers to the severe physical weakness, exhaustion, and deterioration that the body suffers as a result of being starved of food, water, or nourishment over a prolonged period.

This is not simply hunger or tiredness. It is the serious, debilitating condition that results from prolonged deprivation — when the body has been denied the fuel it needs for so long that it begins to break down and lose its ability to function. The body becomes hollow and spent. The person may be too weak to stand, speak clearly, or even stay conscious.

Think of it this way: Imagine a person stranded alone in a desert for eight days, with no food and almost no water. By the time they are rescued, they are not just hungry or thirsty — they are in a state of inanition. Their body has been so completely emptied of what it needs that they are on the verge of collapse.

Example sentences:

  • "The prisoners, denied adequate food for weeks, were found in a state of complete inanition — skeletal, glassy-eyed, and barely alive."
  • "The doctor noted that the patient's inanition was so advanced that even sitting up in bed was beyond her strength."
  • "Relief workers rushing to the famine-stricken village encountered dozens of children suffering from inanition."

Meaning 2 — Figurative (Extended, Less Common)

Inanition can also describe a state of mental, intellectual, or spiritual emptiness — a hollow lifelessness where there is no real energy, substance, or meaning. This is when something (or someone) appears to exist but is completely lacking in vitality, depth, or genuine content.

Think of it this way: Imagine a long, carefully worded political speech that, when you actually listen to it, says absolutely nothing of value. Every sentence sounds polished, but there is no real idea, no substance, no life behind any of it. That speech is a perfect example of inanition.

Example sentences:

  • "His novels, once sharp and bold, had in his later years descended into inanition — pretty sentences with nothing to say."
  • "She had spent so many years in a job that demanded nothing of her mind that a kind of intellectual inanition had quietly settled over her."
  • "The conversation drifted into inanition — polite, pleasant, and utterly empty."

Inanition is not a mild word. It does not describe ordinary tiredness, mild boredom, or slight weakness. It describes a deep, advanced, and serious state of emptiness — whether physical or figurative. In its physical sense, it implies a medical level of deprivation. In its figurative sense, it implies a thoroughgoing hollowness, not just a minor lack of energy.
How It Differs From Similar Words

It helps to see what makes inanition distinct from words that seem close to it.

  • Starvation focuses narrowly on the cause — the lack of food. Inanition focuses on the resulting state — the emptiness and weakness that follows from deprivation of any necessary nourishment (food, water, or even figuratively, meaning and purpose).
  • Exhaustion is broad — you can be exhausted from overwork, illness, stress, or exercise. Inanition specifically points to exhaustion that comes from being drained and emptied of sustenance, not from being overworked.
  • Lethargy means sluggishness and lack of energy, but it doesn't imply the cause or the depth of depletion that inanition does.
  • Weakness is general. Inanition is specific — it tells you why something is weak (because it has been emptied of what sustains it) and implies a serious, advanced degree of that weakness.
The Register: When and Where You'll Encounter This Word

Inanition is a formal, literary, and somewhat medical word. You will not typically hear it in casual everyday conversation. You are most likely to encounter it in:

  • Medical or historical writing — describing the physical condition of starving, malnourished, or severely dehydrated individuals
  • Classic literature and formal prose — where writers use it to describe both physical suffering and spiritual/intellectual hollowness
  • Sophisticated journalism or essays — when a writer wants to precisely describe a deep, draining emptiness in culture, ideas, or public life
Inanition is the serious, debilitating state of emptiness and lifelessness — physical, mental, or spiritual — that results when something is thoroughly deprived of what it needs to sustain itself.
